caseStudies.title: Making a loan application reach a suitable lender
caseStudies.summary: A completed form was not enough. I joined the shared application to lender-specific eligibility and operating follow-through.

sections.title: The challenge
body: An applicant could finish a loan form and still reach a lender whose policy did not fit. The product needed to make lender fit part of the journey without asking the borrower to understand each bank’s requirements.

sections.title: A shared application, with lender-specific routing
body: I chose a common first application rather than a separate journey for each lender. Income band, bureau score, employment type and geography could be captured once and compared with partner eligibility. The alternative was to move policy differences into the borrower’s task: choose a lender first, discover its requirements and repeat work if the fit was wrong.

I established lender-wise MIS and a daily operations view so application progress, partner service levels, payout reconciliation and disputes could be discussed together. Weekly reviews used stage-level drop-offs to decide what needed investigation. A submission acknowledgement, an underwriting decision and a partner payout answered different questions and could not substitute for one another.
sections.title: Operating the handoff
Impact and its limits
body: The documented delivery connected a shared application and eligibility routing to lender onboarding, reporting and commercial follow-through. Lenders retained the credit decision; the product team retained responsibility for understanding the handoff. Available programme figures do not isolate this design or an individual review change, so no release-specific uplift is calculated.

sections.title: A case needs an owner after submission
body: The lesson I carry forward is concrete: a common application helps only if someone can explain whether the case reached its lender, what stopped it and what the partner owes next. That follow-through belonged alongside the product, rather than becoming an unowned queue after launch.

sections.title: Where the shared journey ends and partner policy begins
body: The shared form could not make the lenders interchangeable. Eligibility, the KYC handoff, service commitments and rejection feedback remained lender-specific. I ran those partner conversations alongside engineering’s work on the application, with growth connecting the journey to CashKaro rewards surfaces. That joined the customer-facing entry point to a destination the team could actually operate.

This was a choice about where to handle complexity, not a claim that the platform made a credit decision. Lenders retained review and approval. My responsibility covered the application, routing, partner commercials, operations and P&L; the product boundary extended to understanding what happened after submission.

caseStudies.title: Helping students reach a lender with an assessable case
caseStudies.summary: Students needed more than a loan enquiry: the right evidence, a suitable lender and a clear next step.

sections.title: The challenge
body: An education-loan enquiry is only the beginning. Students still need the right evidence, a suitable lender and a clear next action. Repeated document requests and uncertain handoffs can leave an interested applicant without a case the lender can assess.

sections.title: Prepare a case, not just an enquiry
body: I organized the journey around preparing an assessable case, rather than stopping at lead capture. Common inputs, document collection, eligibility pre-checks and a defined lender handoff formed a thin origination layer. The point was to make case preparation part of the product instead of leaving the applicant to discover the process independently.

I worked with engineering on the application and lender handoff, growth on CashKaro distribution, and operations on submitted cases. MoEngage and internal dashboards exposed abandonment and delay at individual stages. That let the team examine where applicants were getting stuck and whether the next team had usable information, rather than discuss only a final conversion total.

I also owned lender pricing, payout discussions, KYC responsibilities and service levels. More enquiries were useful only if cases could progress at a workable processing cost and satisfy agreed commercial conditions. Loan principal, earned partner revenue and contribution after acquisition and processing costs were different measures. A completed application could not stand in for all three.
sections.title: Connect application reporting to partner operations
Impact and its limits
body: The work connected student information, evidence collection, pre-checks and routing with partner operations and commercials. Comparable cohorts and a reconciled profit figure are unavailable, so this case makes no quantified causal or profitability claim. Public captures show discovery and readiness guidance, not completed offers or lender decisions.

sections.title: Make the next action clear
body: At each handoff, the student and the receiving team need to know what is missing and who acts next. That is the lesson of this work: a completed form matters only when the lender can use the case it receives, and the operating team can follow its progress.

sections.title: Evidence at the next useful step
body: A shorter form can appear successful while passing an incomplete case to the next team. I therefore treated student effort and lender readiness as one design tension. Collecting everything up front would also create unnecessary work; the useful question was what the student needed to provide now and which requirement belonged to the receiving lender or a later step.

The historical education-lending remit included upskilling and tier-2/3 applicants. caseStudies.title: A lending prototype that exposes missing policy
caseStudies.summary: I made missing lender thresholds, uncertain documents and human verification inspectable before allowing a confident match.
caseStudies.role: PRD, rule-model and workflow author; AI-assisted prototyping

sections.title: The challenge
body: Thirteen lender thresholds were missing. A polished interface could still produce a convincing match, but it could not supply the policy evidence behind that answer. I treated those gaps as restrictions on affected-lender release rather than letting the prototype guess.

sections.title: Do not guess missing lender policy
body: I chose deterministic lender gates for the first version and deferred machine-learning scoring until outcome data existed. The alternative would have made a plausible score easier to display while leaving the underlying eligibility uncertain. Relationship-manager confirmation, backed by a policy screenshot, was required before the five affected lenders could be released.

A document can be recognized without its contents being reliable. The design separates classification, validation and verification. For example, an uncertain regional marksheet or scanned tax return must go to a KAM—an account manager reviewing the case—rather than silently becoming verified information. This is the intended handling of the documented example types, not an executed document-quality evaluation.
sections.title: Human verification before matching
Impact and its limits
body: What exists is a documented policy model and original interaction prototype for three roles. The model records 62 rules across eight lender configurations and 23 workflow states; these are scope counts, not correctness scores. Archived software tests cover UI/utilities and locally defined rule helpers, not deployed lender-function correctness or document-model quality. Closure of the recorded release restrictions is not established.

sections.title: Make uncertainty visible before release
body: That choice adds a review step instead of maximizing apparent automation. It also makes unfinished work visible. The archived backlog includes rule-source consistency, a specified Punjab pincode rejection not yet wired into the application, 32 unsecured lender–applicant checklist combinations and a separate operational dashboard. None is presented as subsequently completed.

Before release, I would require approved lender fixtures, verification that cannot be bypassed and matching policy versions across builds. These are proposed gates. Document quality, permissions, score boundaries and recovery need their own evaluation; a software-test pass count cannot establish those results.

sections.title: Deterministic gates before model scoring
body: The model keeps each lender’s conditions visible: eligibility gates first, then a score bounded at 0–100 and five result tiers. Premium-university income exceptions, course factors and urgency adjustments remain policy inputs rather than reasons to improvise an answer. The same verified facts and rule version should produce the same result.

I separated policy exploration from interface scaffolding so each could be inspected independently. AI-assisted building describes how the working artifacts were produced; it does not mean the captured interface runs a live document model or makes a lender’s credit decision. The original role screens use sample data and scripted responses.

sections.title: Different people, different case actions
body: The role views explore different actions against one case model. A student supplies information; a partner submits and manages cases in bulk with payout context; a KAM inspects risk and service-level signals, checks evidence and resolves exceptions. The scripted screenshots show those jobs individually; they are not a recording of one case completing the full journey.

sections.title: Original role views and workflow detail
body: The written student journey has fourteen turns; V1.03 shows a thirteen-step counter. Partners explore bulk submission and payout context. KAMs inspect a queue and verify evidence before rule-engine results. The screenshots are separate scripted role views, not a demonstrated end-to-end execution.

The 23 states describe a workflow state machine, not geography. Lender-by-applicant checklists link document requirements to policy. Uncertain regional marksheets, scanned tax returns and joint statements are documented examples for human review. Expanded coverage and a separate operational KAM dashboard remain archived roadmap items.

decisionBeats.title: Block a confident answer when policy is missing
body: I chose deterministic lender gates for the first version and deferred machine-learning scoring until outcome data existed. The alternative would have made a plausible score easier to display while leaving the underlying eligibility uncertain. Relationship-manager confirmation, backed by a policy screenshot, was required before the five affected lenders could be released.

The model keeps each lender’s conditions visible: eligibility gates first, then a score bounded at 0–100 and five result tiers. Premium-university income exceptions, course factors and urgency adjustments remain policy inputs rather than reasons to improvise an answer. The same verified facts and rule version should produce the same result.

I separated policy exploration from interface scaffolding so each could be inspected independently. AI-assisted building describes how the working artifacts were produced; it does not mean the captured interface runs a live document model or makes a lender’s credit decision. The original role screens use sample data and scripted responses.

decisionBeats.title: Make verification a real handoff
body: A document can be recognized without its contents being reliable. The design separates classification, validation and verification. For example, an uncertain regional marksheet or scanned tax return must go to a KAM—an account manager reviewing the case—rather than silently becoming verified information. This is the intended handling of the documented example types, not an executed document-quality evaluation.

The role views explore different actions against one case model. A student supplies information; a partner submits and manages cases in bulk with payout context; a KAM inspects risk and service-level signals, checks evidence and resolves exceptions. The scripted screenshots show those jobs individually; they are not a recording of one case completing the full journey.

That choice adds a review step instead of maximizing apparent automation. It also makes unfinished work visible. The archived backlog includes rule-source consistency, a specified Punjab pincode rejection not yet wired into the application, 32 unsecured lender–applicant checklist combinations and a separate operational dashboard. None is presented as subsequently completed.

Before release, I would require approved lender fixtures, verification that cannot be bypassed and matching policy versions across builds. These are proposed gates. Document quality, permissions, score boundaries and recovery need their own evaluation; a software-test pass count cannot establish those results.

sections.title: Shared structure without erasing partner meaning
body: I identified eligibility, KYC handoff, application status and payout information as recurring concerns across lender connections. I worked with engineering on a common structure and with lender teams on policy, responsibilities and service commitments. That was an alternative to making each new partner another unrelated borrower journey.

I worked directly with engineering and partners on the modular lending stack, KYC responsibility, service levels and commercials. Rejection feedback could inform routing and product priorities. I also recruited across product, sales and operations, helping build the cross-functional capability for continuing partner follow-through.

Daily MIS joined lender-wise funnel performance, service-level tracking, payout reconciliation and disputes. The operating question continued after a request was accepted: which case was waiting, which partner commitment needed attention, and which commercial record remained unresolved? Those queues belonged in partner reviews as well as in the interface.

sections.title: The challenge
body: If a chat and reviewer tool depend on the same lending policy, separate rule implementations can disagree or require duplicate updates. I explored a common evaluation boundary; cross-interface demand and the choice of transport still need validation.

sections.title: One proposed policy boundary
body: I proposed letting intended clients—the student interaction, reviewer tools and possible future interfaces—ask the same versioned lending-policy service for an evaluation. The architecture direction places two business-rule engines behind one Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. A business-rule engine applies the explicit eligibility and scoring policy; MCP is one possible interface for exposing that capability to tool-using clients.

A lender rejection might indicate missing information, unsuitable routing or an outdated rule. In an illustrative review, the first task is to identify which explanation fits the original case and policy version. A rejection should create evidence for investigation; it should not silently alter the next applicant’s evaluation.
sections.title: Diagnose feedback before changing policy

body: What exists is an architecture direction and later authored contract/control examples. Live MCP wiring, consumer reuse, production authorization and the approval/rollback process are unverified. This exploration claims no achieved business result, live integration or automatic policy-retuning capability.

sections.title: Explain a decision without rewriting the rule
body: A system can explain today’s evaluation without being allowed to rewrite tomorrow’s policy. Before a release claim, I would require consistent results for authorized inputs and versions, explicit failure handling without fabricated decisions, and reviewed changes with rollback. These are proposed checks, not measured results.

sections.title: The contract and the conventional API alternative
body: An illustrative contract takes an authorized, verified case and an explicit product and policy version. A chat and a reviewer could present the answer differently while receiving the same pre-check reasons and missing-input flags. This is a proposed example, not an executed cross-client comparison or a lender approval.

A conventional service API is a real alternative. Shared evaluation does not require MCP by itself. MCP would earn its added interface and authorization work only if intended tool-using clients need it and the service can demonstrate consistent versioned behaviour. That choice remains unresolved rather than being presented as an architectural inevitability.

sections.title: Consumer evaluation is not administrative approval
body: I separated consumer evaluation from privileged policy change. Feedback can create a review item, but approval belongs to a separately authorized human workflow. The precise owner, operating procedure, version history and rollback mechanism still need to be defined and tested. Ordinary applicant clients must not inherit that authority.

decisionBeats.title: Reuse an evaluation, not an interface
body: I proposed letting intended clients—the student interaction, reviewer tools and possible future interfaces—ask the same versioned lending-policy service for an evaluation. The architecture direction places two business-rule engines behind one Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. A business-rule engine applies the explicit eligibility and scoring policy; MCP is one possible interface for exposing that capability to tool-using clients.

An illustrative contract takes an authorized, verified case and an explicit product and policy version. A chat and a reviewer could present the answer differently while receiving the same pre-check reasons and missing-input flags. This is a proposed example, not an executed cross-client comparison or a lender approval.

A conventional service API is a real alternative. Shared evaluation does not require MCP by itself. decisionBeats.title: Feedback requests review; it does not change policy
body: A lender rejection might indicate missing information, unsuitable routing or an outdated rule. In an illustrative review, the first task is to identify which explanation fits the original case and policy version. A rejection should create evidence for investigation; it should not silently alter the next applicant’s evaluation.

I separated consumer evaluation from privileged policy change. Feedback can create a review item, but approval belongs to a separately authorized human workflow. The precise owner, operating procedure, version history and rollback mechanism still need to be defined and tested. Ordinary applicant clients must not inherit that authority.

A system can explain today’s evaluation without being allowed to rewrite tomorrow’s policy. Before a release claim, I would require consistent results for authorized inputs and versions, explicit failure handling without fabricated decisions, and reviewed changes with rollback. sections.title: Capture evidence without waiting for a network
body: The delivered flow let a farmer photograph a leaf offline and receive the diagnosis when the phone reconnected. That separated evidence collection from connection availability, rather than require both to happen at the same moment.

The requirement was not simply a smaller grid cell. I worked on connecting that output to the local information an actuarial team could use in premium tables. The evidence does not provide a publishable acceptance threshold or show that every finer cell was more accurate.

caseStudies.title: UrbanKhet: the business behind a fresh-produce order
caseStudies.summary: I founded UrbanKhet, moving from terrace farming into produce delivery and owning the web product, sourcing, fulfilment and P&L.

sections.title: From growing food to delivering it
body: UrbanKhet began with terrace farming. I moved towards direct produce supply for people who wanted fresh food without growing it themselves. That changed what we had to deliver: an order was a commitment to source, pack and transport something perishable, not simply a sale on a website.

sections.title: Building the produce service
body: I acquired the first 44 customers manually and developed farmer supply through cold outreach and local relationships. I then built household subscriptions and business supply around that sourcing operation.

The web product, customer acquisition, distribution and P&L were my founder responsibilities. The business account reports a 28-person team and names Marriott, BigBasket, Udaan and Ninjacart among its business customers.

I built the web product and operating workflows for decentralised distribution in Maharashtra and Gujarat. Sourcing, inventory, harvest timing and last-mile delivery had to keep pace with the customer order. I established SOPs to make the routines repeatable across the team.

The historical storefront shows the customer side of those commitments: choose produce, assemble a pack and select a delivery plan. It shows the ordering experience; fulfilment performance is recorded separately.
sections.title: Connecting the order to fulfilment
What the venture became
body: UrbanKhet operated household subscriptions alongside B2B produce supply. I owned the product and the operation behind those relationships, including acquisition, sourcing, fulfilment and P&L.

The founder records report a 28-person team. Customer and farmer totals cover different periods and definitions, so they are retained in the detailed evidence rather than presented as a single growth, retention or profit result.

sections.title: The perspective I bring to commerce
body: This work made me examine an online promise alongside the people, inventory and delivery work needed to keep it. That is the perspective I bring to commerce and service products whose customer experience extends beyond the screen.

sections.title: From early customers to a household offer
body: I acquired the first 44 customers manually, alongside farmer outreach and local relationships. Household subscriptions and business supply developed around the same sourcing operation.

The original Sorted-Packs post of 10 April 2020 shows curated vegetable combinations and household proportions. The Khet Direct launch of 20 October 2020 shows a wider range of subscription packs and an eight-hour harvest-to-home promise. These are dated customer propositions, rather than measured delivery or retention results.

sections.title: The operating model and its reported limits
body: I developed the web product and routines for sourcing, inventory, harvest and last-mile delivery, with decentralised urban distribution in Maharashtra and Gujarat. Household and business orders depended on those handoffs.

The March 2022 career record reports maximum wastage of 10%, compared with an asserted 35% industry benchmark. This is an operating level, not a measured before-and-after reduction. A later founder account describes six-hour harvest-to-home delivery; the October 2020 company launch post promised eight hours. The accounts refer to different versions of the service.

The direct and intermediary-chain graphics are UrbanKhet’s original marketing explanations from 5 November 2019. They explain the company’s proposition, not its actual SOPs or independently verified supply-chain performance.

body: The public origin story traces a microfarm model involving a space owner, an investor and a technical operator in 2018. My formal Founder & Director tenure in the CV is July 2019–September 2021.

A GUSEC interview and Startup Gujarat newsletter documented produce delivery in June 2020. GUSEC’s 2020–21 snapshot records Continuity Accelerator support and unit-economics mentoring. The chronology below retains the publication, award and campaign dates for readers examining the venture’s history.

decisionBeats.title: From the first customers to household packs
body: I acquired the first 44 customers manually. Farmer supply developed through cold outreach and local relationships, so I was building the two sides of the service before there was an established customer base. Moving from terrace farming into produce supply meant taking responsibility for what arrived at someone’s door, rather than asking that customer to do the growing.

I built household subscriptions and business supply around that operation. They were different relationships: a household pack served a recurring domestic need, while a hotel or marketplace ordered for a different volume and specification. Both still depended on the same perishable supply reaching the customer in usable condition.

The two company posts show the offer at different moments. Sorted-Packs, published in April 2020, explains curated vegetable combinations and household proportions. The October 2020 Khet Direct launch presents subscription packs and an eight-hour harvest-to-home promise. They show how the service was packaged and communicated; they do not tell us which campaign caused demand or whether every delivery met its promise.

decisionBeats.title: Making the order work beyond the screen
body: I built the web product and operating workflows for decentralised distribution in Maharashtra and Gujarat. An order connected sourcing, inventory, harvest timing, packing and last-mile delivery. A customer-facing pack or delivery choice therefore had an operating commitment behind it, and I owned both sides as founder.

In the storefront excerpt, watch the move from produce to a custom pack and then to the cart, alongside the delivery calendar. That is the visible customer journey. The corresponding work was organising the supply and fulfilment routines needed to keep the order moving. I established SOPs and coordinated the team rather than treating the website as a separate finished project.

My responsibilities included acquisition, farmer relationships, business development, fulfilment and P&L. The founder account reports a 28-person team and names Marriott, BigBasket, Udaan and Ninjacart among business customers. Those details describe operating scope, rather than proving an isolated product effect.

The later COVID response and wind-down are a separate part of this story. I changed the demand and delivery model during the first wave, then later faced the question of whether the business could continue. The companion case follows those two periods.

body: You may have a product idea without a clear first customer, or customer interest without a workable cost to serve. Those are connected questions I can help structure before the roadmap expands.

sections.title: A proposed way of working
body: For a new engagement, we would start with one decision: whom to serve first, what to offer, what delivery costs or how to reach customers. We would separate evidence from assumptions, compare options and identify a useful next test.
The proposed output is a short decision brief: the question, constraints, evidence, options and next test. Its scope would depend on the actual problem, rather than a universal packaged deliverable.

My independent advisory subjects have included zero-to-one product direction, unit economics, go-to-market and fundraising narrative across FMCG, energy and carbon-credit ventures. Client details remain private.
The disclosed UrbanKhet and platform cases show the operating experience I bring. They are proof of my own founder and product work, not advisory-client outcomes.
sections.title: The experience I would bring
A hypothetical working sample
body: Imagine a household-subscription product deciding between a fixed weekly pack and custom orders. In a working session, I would compare the customer need, available supply, packing effort, delivery density and evidence of willingness to reorder.

The output could be a comparison of the options and a small test of the uncertain assumption. This is an illustrative method sample, not a past client engagement, adopted recommendation or promised result. No example prices, margins or performance figures are assumed.

sections.title: FC Sparta at CEPT
body: At CEPT, I captained FC Sparta during a run of three consecutive championships. The team had finished near the bottom before that run. The wins were the team’s achievement.
I paint alongside my professional work. The Art collection shows six original works, with close-ups, materials, dimensions and the notes that accompanied them.
Public Compass is oil on canvas. Tumult, Continual and Live-life combine oil and acrylic; Celestial is acrylic, and Reminiscence is charcoal.
